description: OVIKORSHO is a team of programmers and space enthusiasts exploring the universe through NASA data and technology. We work across astrophysics, astronomy, AI, data science, and software development to investigate complex problems, uncover patterns, and turn space data into meaningful discoveries and interactive solutions.
summary:
Martis helps astronauts and robotic missions navigate safely, assess risks, and conduct science on Mars. With 4–24-minute one-way communication delays, crews must act independently. It combines terrain-aware A-star path planning using 200 m USGS, HRSC, and MOLA elevation data with soil terramechanics, slope hazards, VHF line-of-sight analysis, and Point-of-No-Return walkback contours to keep EVAs within oxygen and metabolic limits. Its resource layer integrates Mars Odyssey GRS elemental maps, 1,062 USGS cave-shelter candidates, 1,000+ PSI dust-storm tracks, 4,200+ sols of Curiosity radiation data, MEDA/REMS/APSS weather, and 129 km of rover traverses across five NASA surface missions.

The In-Situ Science Lab analyzes 20 Jezero rock targets and 18,500+ spectral records across six modules, drawing on PIXL, SuperCam LIBS, and SHERLOC approaches, plus the 24-tube Mars Sample Return depot manifest. Eight machine-learning models classify geochemistry, detect astrobiological anomalies, and predict solar-array degradation, calibrated on 5,352 Opportunity and 1,440 InSight sols. A helmet HUD, JPL Horizons-based orbiter relay-pass predictions, and a multimodal EVA assistant support operations. Planned additions include hazard detection from high-resolution imagery, scout-drone support, and autonomous sweep navigation. By boosting crew autonomy, reducing reliance on Earth, and linking safety with science, Martis aims to enable safer, more sustainable Mars exploration.
details:
Martis is an integrated Mars exploration and mission-support platform designed to make future human surface missions safer, smarter, and more independent. With communication delays of up to 22 minutes one way between Earth and Mars, astronauts cannot always rely on immediate guidance from Mission Control. Martis addresses this challenge by bringing essential navigation, scientific analysis, and mission decision-making directly to the Martian surface.

At its core, Martis combines interactive 2D and 3D planetary mapping with authentic NASA and USGS datasets, providing detailed terrain visualization, energy-efficient route planning, slope and hazard assessment, and dynamic Point-of-No-Return (PNR) safety boundaries based on astronaut oxygen and life-support reserves. It also integrates real rover traverses, landing-site analysis, resource mapping, and environmental monitoring to support informed surface operations.

Beyond navigation, Martis features an interactive In-Situ Science Lab that models scientific instruments and analytical workflows from NASA's Perseverance and Curiosity missions. Its eight-family machine-learning engine, comprising 33 sub-models, runs directly in the browser to support atmospheric forecasting, dust-storm tracking, geochemical classification, radiation assessment, and astrobiological anomaly detection. Additional capabilities include a contingency simulator, orbital dynamics and communication monitoring, high-resolution NASA imagery exploration, and a collaborative astronaut community hub with an intelligent EVA copilot.

Built with modern web technologies, CesiumJS, Leaflet, Web Workers, JavaScript-based ML models, and a Supabase cloud backend, Martis combines scientific data with interactive mission tools. Its route-planning system has also been validated against 76 km of actual Perseverance and Curiosity rover traverse data. A scientific truth framework distinguishes authentic mission observations, empirical ML predictions, and physics-based estimates.

Looking ahead, Martis aims to expand into high-resolution orbital hazard detection, autonomous scout-drone integration, dynamic surface rerouting, and direct spacesuit telemetry integration. Our vision is to bridge orbital reconnaissance and surface exploration, giving future crews the intelligence and independence to explore farther, make better decisions, and always find their way home.
